blocks.text: A resistor R is connected to an AC source (Fig 17.6 a). The instantaneous voltage is V = Vo sin(wt) (17.10), and the current is I = V/R = (Vo/R) sin(wt) = Io sin(wt) (17.11), where Io = Vo/R is the peak current. Voltage and current are both sine functions that pass their maximum and minimum values at the same time, so they are in phase (Fig 17.6 b). In the phasor diagram the vectors VR and IR are drawn parallel (Fig 17.6 c). The opposition to the current is the resistance, R = V/I.

blocks.alt: (a) A resistor R in a loop with an AC source V. (b) Voltage V (green) and current I (purple) against time, crossing zero together at pi and 2 pi and peaking together: in phase. (c) Two parallel arrows of the same direction, VR and IR.
blocks.caption: Figure 17.6: (a) A resistor R connected with an AC source; (b) graph for a purely resistive circuit showing V and I in phase; (c) VR and IR vectors for a resistance (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 17.6).

The power dissipated is proportional to the square of the current, so it does not matter whether the current is positive or negative. But an AC of peak Io does not dissipate as much power as a DC of value Io, because the AC is at its peak only for an instant in each half-cycle. The instantaneous power is P = VI = I^2 R = V^2/R (17.12). The average power is

= R, and since = Io^2/2 = Irms^2,

= Irms^2 R = Irms Vrms. These formulas hold only when V and I are in phase.

blocks.title: For your information
blocks.text: Many video doorbells run on 12 V AC: low-voltage AC is safer to handle and reduces the risk of electric shock.

A 1 kW heating element is connected to a 250 V AC supply. Find the current taken from the supply and the resistance of the element when hot. Solution: P = VI, so I = P/V = 1000 W / 250 V = 4 A, and R = V/I = 250 V / 4 A = 62.5 ohm.
